Both block dopamine. See the dopamine-blocker rule.

All of these block central D2 receptors. Stack two and the blockade deepens, and so does every consequence of it: extrapyramidal symptoms, akathisia, tardive dyskinesia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

The pairing that gets missed is an antipsychotic patient who is then given metoclopramide or prochlorperazine for nausea. Ondansetron does not block dopamine and is the safer antiemetic in that patient.

After each beat the ventricle has to repolarize, meaning reset its electrical charge, before it can beat again. Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what does that. These drugs block hERG, so repolarization drags out. That dragged-out reset is what a long QT measures, and a beat firing during that stretched window can tip the rhythm into torsades de pointes.

They do not all carry the same weight. Ondansetron, methadone, prochlorperazine, chlorpromazine, haloperidol, amitriptyline, the fluoroquinolones and the macrolides, Bactrim, and the antiarrhythmics amiodarone and procainamide are the established ones. Loperamide belongs here only at HIGHER THAN RECOMMENDED doses, which is what its boxed warning is about. For the antiarrhythmics the QT effect IS the mechanism, not a side effect, which is why a class IA or class III drug can treat an arrhythmia and cause torsades with the same action. Escitalopram, quetiapine and olanzapine prolong QT only modestly (escitalopram by about 7 msec at 20 mg), and for metronidazole the evidence is case reports while fluoxetine's effect is marginal, so treat all of those as a reason to check rather than a reason to expect it.

The SSRI with a genuinely QT-driven dose restriction is CITALOPRAM, not escitalopram.
Both shift the balance slightly. Worth noticing, and worth acting on only if the patient has another risk factor: a seizure history, withdrawal, head injury, hyponatremia or an eating disorder.

Each of these blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. One drug gives you a dry mouth. Two or three give you the full picture: blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, blocked sweating so heat cannot be shed, and in older adults an acute confusion that gets charted as dementia or a UTI rather than as the drugs.

The clinical point is that total load matters, not any single drug. This is what the Beers criteria are built around, and it is the most common reversible cause of delirium in a hospitalized older adult.

The three that most often go uncounted are DIPHENHYDRAMINE (in sleep aids and cold remedies the patient does not call medication), BENZTROPINE (given to treat the side effects of an antipsychotic that is itself anticholinergic), and PROMETHAZINE. Add any two and an older adult is at real risk.
Two antipsychotics. See the dopamine-blocker rule.

SELECTIVITY decides this one. Propranolol and carvedilol block beta-2 as well as beta-1, so the rescue inhaler stops working and the blocker itself can cause bronchospasm. In asthma this is the classic contraindicated pairing.

Every heartbeat starts at the SA node and has to pass the AV node to reach the ventricle. Both nodes depend on calcium moving slowly into the cell, and on sympathetic tone to speed that up. Each drug here takes away one of those, by a different route, and the nodes do not care which route it was: the rate falls, and conduction through the AV node stretches out until a beat is dropped.

Beta blockers slow both nodes by removing the sympathetic drive. Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers slow the same nodes by blocking the calcium entry itself. Two different doors into the same room. Amiodarone, digoxin and lacosamide reach those nodes by three more routes. Most of these combinations are deliberate rate control rather than errors, so the question is almost never whether to allow the pair but what hold parameter is written and whether anyone looked at an ECG. The one pairing that genuinely stands out is a beta blocker with diltiazem or verapamil.

A labeled contraindication. PTU blocks ORGANIFICATION, so the radioiodine is taken up and then washes out before it can deliver its dose, and the treatment fails. PTU is held for several days beforehand and often resumed afterward while waiting for the effect.
Same: ↓ level → clot risk, labeled avoid, and no level to monitor.
Same opposition.
Two statins. Pick one.

Every drug here can injure skeletal muscle, by routes that are mostly still argued about, and stacking two raises the chance. The sequence is what to hold on to: aching, then tenderness and weakness, then muscle breaking down fast enough to block the kidneys. The first step sounds exactly like having overdone it at the gym, which is why patients do not report it.

Statins, fibrates and niacin each injure muscle on their own, and together the risk climbs. Muscle pain and weakness are the warning. Rhabdomyolysis is the endpoint: muscle breaking down fast enough to damage the kidneys.

Why this is moderate and not high: the fibrate behind the serious cases is GEMFIBROZIL, which slows how fast the body clears a statin, so the statin builds up. Fenofibrate does not do that, which is exactly why it is the fibrate you pair with a statin. Gemfibrozil is not in this set.

How statins injure muscle at all is still unsettled. The leading explanation is that the pathway they block also supplies coenzyme Q10 to muscle.

Direct antagonism. Streptokinase generates plasmin to dissolve clot; tranexamic acid blocks plasmin formation. TXA is in fact the RESCUE for serious streptokinase bleeding, so giving them together outside that rescue cancels the therapy.
Same opposition.
Both injure the tubule directly. IV acyclovir alongside gentamicin or vancomycin is a real stack: creatinine daily, hydrate, and question whether both are still needed.

The one that gets missed. The diuretic removes total body potassium and the beta-2 agonist hides how low it has gone by shifting what is left into cells, so the level understates the deficit and overstates it in turn as the drug wears off. Back-to-back nebulizers in a patient on furosemide is the scenario. Check K⁺ and Mg²⁺ together.

Standard asthma and COPD therapy, not an error. Both halves lower the potassium by different routes, the steroid by trading it away and the agonist by shifting it, so an exacerbation treated with repeated nebulizers plus prednisone is a real hypokalemia risk. Check a K⁺.

The potassium does not have to leave the body to make digoxin toxic. What the Na+/K+ pump competes with is the potassium in the SERUM, so insulin, bicarbonate or a beta-2 nebulizer driving it into cells frees up binding sites within the hour, and a level that reads therapeutic starts behaving like an overdose. Two things follow. Treating hyperkalemia in a digitalized patient can tip them into toxicity, so the ECG matters as much as the next potassium. And the number comes back up on its own as the drug wears off, so a single low K⁺ drawn mid-nebulizer is not the whole picture.

Common in acute agitation and often appropriate, but the sedation, the orthostatic hypotension and the fall risk all add. Monitor respiratory rate, not just whether the patient settled.

These inhibitors block the enzyme that clears the substrates, so the substrate accumulates at an unchanged dose. CYCLOSPORINE is in both roles: it inhibits CYP3A4 and OATP1B1, and it is itself a 3A4 substrate, so its level swings with anything that touches the enzyme and it raises the levels of others.

Erythromycin is the one the labels treat as potent: the methylergonovine label names it among the potent CYP3A4 inhibitors and the simvastatin label groups the macrolides with the contraindicated ones. FDA's own clinical-pharmacology classification puts it with diltiazem and verapamil as MODERATE, so read the word potent here as the labels' practical judgment rather than a tier. Amlodipine is a WEAK inhibitor and is not listed here: its one labeled consequence is the simvastatin 20 mg cap, which is carried as a named pair in the miscellaneous rule.

Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.

After each beat the ventricle has to repolarize, meaning reset its electrical charge, before it can beat again. Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what does that. These drugs block hERG, so repolarization drags out. That dragged-out reset is what a long QT measures, and a beat firing during that stretched window can tip the rhythm into torsades de pointes.

They do not all carry the same weight. Ondansetron, methadone, prochlorperazine, chlorpromazine, haloperidol, amitriptyline, the fluoroquinolones and the macrolides, Bactrim, and the antiarrhythmics amiodarone and procainamide are the established ones. Loperamide belongs here only at HIGHER THAN RECOMMENDED doses, which is what its boxed warning is about. For the antiarrhythmics the QT effect IS the mechanism, not a side effect, which is why a class IA or class III drug can treat an arrhythmia and cause torsades with the same action. Escitalopram, quetiapine and olanzapine prolong QT only modestly (escitalopram by about 7 msec at 20 mg), and for metronidazole the evidence is case reports while fluoxetine's effect is marginal, so treat all of those as a reason to check rather than a reason to expect it.

The SSRI with a genuinely QT-driven dose restriction is CITALOPRAM, not escitalopram.

Two problems at once: bupropion inhibits CYP2D6 so the amitriptyline level climbs, and both drugs lower the seizure threshold. Amitriptyline has a narrow margin and its toxicity is cardiac, so this is a level worth measuring.

A seizure happens when excitation outruns inhibition. Several of these drugs shift that balance a little: bupropion by raising dopamine and norepinephrine, the antipsychotics by blocking dopamine, the tricyclics through multiple receptors, methylphenidate by raising catecholamines, and the fluoroquinolones by blocking GABA-A directly.

One of them alone rarely causes a seizure in a patient with no risk factors. Stacked, or added to withdrawal, head injury, hyponatremia, an eating disorder or a prior seizure, the margin gets thin. Bupropion is the one that matters most, which is why it is in its own group.

After each beat the ventricle has to repolarize, meaning reset its electrical charge, before it can beat again. Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what does that. These drugs block hERG, so repolarization drags out. That dragged-out reset is what a long QT measures, and a beat firing during that stretched window can tip the rhythm into torsades de pointes.

Two or three give you the full picture: blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, blocked sweating so heat cannot be shed, and in older adults an acute confusion that gets charted as dementia or a UTI rather than as the drugs.

The three that most often go uncounted are DIPHENHYDRAMINE (in sleep aids and cold remedies the patient does not call medication), BENZTROPINE (given to treat the side effects of an antipsychotic that is itself anticholinergic), and PROMETHAZINE. Add any two and an older adult is at real risk.

After each beat the ventricle has to repolarize, meaning reset its electrical charge, before it can beat again. Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what does that. These drugs block hERG, so repolarization drags out. That dragged-out reset is what a long QT measures, and a beat firing during that stretched window can tip the rhythm into torsades de pointes.

They do not all carry the same weight. Ondansetron, methadone, prochlorperazine, chlorpromazine, haloperidol, amitriptyline, the fluoroquinolones and the macrolides, Bactrim, and the antiarrhythmics amiodarone and procainamide are the established ones. Loperamide belongs here only at HIGHER THAN RECOMMENDED doses, which is what its boxed warning is about. For the antiarrhythmics the QT effect IS the mechanism, not a side effect, which is why a class IA or class III drug can treat an arrhythmia and cause torsades with the same action. Escitalopram, quetiapine and olanzapine prolong QT only modestly (escitalopram by about 7 msec at 20 mg), and for metronidazole the evidence is case reports while fluoxetine's effect is marginal, so treat all of those as a reason to check rather than a reason to expect it.

The SSRI with a genuinely QT-driven dose restriction is CITALOPRAM, not escitalopram.
Both shift the balance slightly. Worth noticing, and worth acting on only if the patient has another risk factor: a seizure history, withdrawal, head injury, hyponatremia or an eating disorder.

Low K+ and low Mg2+ lengthen the QT on their own, so they stack with a QT drug. Scoped to loop diuretics, steroids and stimulant laxatives, which drop TOTAL BODY potassium. Insulin, bicarbonate and a beta-2 agonist shift potassium into cells rather than removing it, and at routine dosing that shift is not a torsades risk on its own.

Labeled on the amlodipine side: co-administration with a moderate or strong CYP3A inhibitor raises amlodipine exposure, and diltiazem did so in the studies. Two routes. All of them kill the gut bacteria that make vitamin K, which is the vitamin warfarin already works against, so the warfarin effect deepens. Metronidazole, Bactrim, erythromycin and isoniazid do something extra: they also block the enzyme that clears warfarin, so the drug itself builds up. Two hits instead of one is why those push the INR hardest.

RIFAMPIN is the exception that reverses the whole rule. It INDUCES the enzyme instead of blocking it, so the INR FALLS and the patient clots while looking anticoagulated on paper. See the induction rule.

Beta-lactams chemically INACTIVATE aminoglycosides on contact. In the patient the two are synergistic and deliberately combined, which is standard therapy in endocarditis. In the same syringe, bag or running line they destroy each other and the patient gets a fraction of the aminoglycoside dose.

So this is not a reason to avoid the combination. It is a reason to separate the administration: different times, flushed line, or a second access.

Scoped to PARENTERAL penicillins, because the interaction is physical. An oral cephalosporin or oral amoxicillin never shares a line with IV gentamicin, so there is nothing to inactivate. The documented chemistry is a penicillin-class reaction, not a cephalosporin one.

Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.

Bismuth subsalicylate IS a salicylate, so the hazard with warfarin or any anticoagulant is additive BLEEDING and a rising INR, not reduced absorption. Patients do not think of Pepto-Bismol as medication, let alone as aspirin, so it has to be asked about by name.

These inhibitors block the enzyme that clears the substrates, so the substrate accumulates at an unchanged dose. CYCLOSPORINE is in both roles: it inhibits CYP3A4 and OATP1B1, and it is itself a 3A4 substrate, so its level swings with anything that touches the enzyme and it raises the levels of others.

Erythromycin is the one the labels treat as potent: the methylergonovine label names it among the potent CYP3A4 inhibitors and the simvastatin label groups the macrolides with the contraindicated ones. FDA's own clinical-pharmacology classification puts it with diltiazem and verapamil as MODERATE, so read the word potent here as the labels' practical judgment rather than a tier. Amlodipine is a WEAK inhibitor and is not listed here: its one labeled consequence is the simvastatin 20 mg cap, which is carried as a named pair in the miscellaneous rule.

Two anticoagulants may be a deliberate BRIDGE (heparin or enoxaparin overlapping warfarin until the INR is therapeutic; the 5-day parenteral lead-in dabigatran requires) or a duplication. Judge by the plan, not the count.

The stomach lining defends itself three ways: a mucus and bicarbonate layer, blood flow to repair what gets through, and platelets to stop a bleed once one starts. Each drug here removes a different one of those, so two of them together take away both the defence and the repair.

NSAIDs remove the prostaglandins that build the mucus layer and keep the blood flowing. Steroids impair mucosal healing and mask the pain that would have warned you. SSRIs deplete platelet serotonin, so when a vessel does open there is less to plug it with: the ulcer risk they add is small, and the BLEEDING risk is the real one.

NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.

The stomach lining defends itself three ways: a mucus and bicarbonate layer, blood flow to repair what gets through, and platelets to stop a bleed once one starts. Each drug here removes a different one of those, so two of them together take away both the defence and the repair.

NSAIDs remove the prostaglandins that build the mucus layer and keep the blood flowing. Steroids impair mucosal healing and mask the pain that would have warned you. SSRIs deplete platelet serotonin, so when a vessel does open there is less to plug it with: the ulcer risk they add is small, and the BLEEDING risk is the real one.

A beta blocker with digoxin is STANDARD therapy in atrial fibrillation and heart failure, not a contraindication. Both slow AV conduction, so monitor the rate and write a hold parameter.

A beta blocker works by sitting on the receptor. Anything else you give that needs the SAME receptor then has to compete for it, so the dose that normally works does less than expected, and how much less depends on which receptor and how selective the blocker is. That cuts two ways in this rule: a pressor that cannot raise the pressure, and a rescue inhaler that cannot open the airway.

Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine and dobutamine all work through adrenergic receptors. A beta blocker already occupying those receptors reduces the response. With epinephrine the picture is worse: beta blockade leaves alpha effects unopposed, which can produce severe hypertension with reflex bradycardia.

These inhibitors block the enzyme that clears the substrates, so the substrate accumulates at an unchanged dose. CYCLOSPORINE is in both roles: it inhibits CYP3A4 and OATP1B1, and it is itself a 3A4 substrate, so its level swings with anything that touches the enzyme and it raises the levels of others.

Erythromycin is the one the labels treat as potent: the methylergonovine label names it among the potent CYP3A4 inhibitors and the simvastatin label groups the macrolides with the contraindicated ones. FDA's own clinical-pharmacology classification puts it with diltiazem and verapamil as MODERATE, so read the word potent here as the labels' practical judgment rather than a tier. Amlodipine is a WEAK inhibitor and is not listed here: its one labeled consequence is the simvastatin 20 mg cap, which is carried as a named pair in the miscellaneous rule.
Same mechanism, and atorvastatin is also CYP3A4-cleared, but it is not a labeled contraindication. Watch for muscle pain and consider holding it.

Low K+ and low Mg2+ lengthen the QT on their own, so they stack with a QT drug. Scoped to loop diuretics, steroids and stimulant laxatives, which drop TOTAL BODY potassium. Insulin, bicarbonate and a beta-2 agonist shift potassium into cells rather than removing it, and at routine dosing that shift is not a torsades risk on its own.

After each beat the ventricle has to repolarize, meaning reset its electrical charge, before it can beat again. Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what does that. These drugs block hERG, so repolarization drags out. That dragged-out reset is what a long QT measures, and a beat firing during that stretched window can tip the rhythm into torsades de pointes.

They do not all carry the same weight. Ondansetron, methadone, prochlorperazine, chlorpromazine, haloperidol, amitriptyline, the fluoroquinolones and the macrolides, Bactrim, and the antiarrhythmics amiodarone and procainamide are the established ones. Loperamide belongs here only at HIGHER THAN RECOMMENDED doses, which is what its boxed warning is about. For the antiarrhythmics the QT effect IS the mechanism, not a side effect, which is why a class IA or class III drug can treat an arrhythmia and cause torsades with the same action. Escitalopram, quetiapine and olanzapine prolong QT only modestly (escitalopram by about 7 msec at 20 mg), and for metronidazole the evidence is case reports while fluoxetine's effect is marginal, so treat all of those as a reason to check rather than a reason to expect it.

The SSRI with a genuinely QT-driven dose restriction is CITALOPRAM, not escitalopram.

After each beat the ventricle has to repolarize, meaning reset its electrical charge, before it can beat again. Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what does that. These drugs block hERG, so repolarization drags out. That dragged-out reset is what a long QT measures, and a beat firing during that stretched window can tip the rhythm into torsades de pointes.

Two routes. All of them kill the gut bacteria that make vitamin K, which is the vitamin warfarin already works against, so the warfarin effect deepens. Metronidazole, Bactrim, erythromycin and isoniazid do something extra: they also block the enzyme that clears warfarin, so the drug itself builds up. Two hits instead of one is why those push the INR hardest.

RIFAMPIN is the exception that reverses the whole rule. It INDUCES the enzyme instead of blocking it, so the INR FALLS and the patient clots while looking anticoagulated on paper. See the induction rule.

Potassium can leave the blood two ways, and the lab draw looks the same either way. It can leave the BODY, through the kidney or the gut, which is a true deficit that has to be replaced. Or it can move INTO the cells, which is a shift that reverses on its own when the drug wears off. Replacing a shift overshoots; ignoring a deficit does not correct.

Loop diuretics dump K⁺ at the loop of Henle. Prednisone, methylprednisolone and cortisone hold Na⁺ and trade away K⁺ through mineralocorticoid activity. Dexamethasone has almost none of that activity, so its hypokalemia is weaker and arrives by other routes at high dose, which is why it sits in a group of its own here. Insulin, sodium bicarbonate and a beta-2 agonist don't remove potassium at all, they drive it into cells, which looks identical on a lab draw and corrects itself when the drug wears off.

A seizure happens when excitation outruns inhibition. Several of these drugs shift that balance a little: bupropion by raising dopamine and norepinephrine, the antipsychotics by blocking dopamine, the tricyclics through multiple receptors, methylphenidate by raising catecholamines, and the fluoroquinolones by blocking GABA-A directly.

One of them alone rarely causes a seizure in a patient with no risk factors. Stacked, or added to withdrawal, head injury, hyponatremia, an eating disorder or a prior seizure, the margin gets thin. Bupropion is the one that matters most, which is why it is in its own group.
Bupropion plus a fluoroquinolone stacks the strongest seizure-threshold drug in the set with a labeled CNS-stimulant antibiotic.

These inhibitors block the enzyme that clears the substrates, so the substrate accumulates at an unchanged dose. CYCLOSPORINE is in both roles: it inhibits CYP3A4 and OATP1B1, and it is itself a 3A4 substrate, so its level swings with anything that touches the enzyme and it raises the levels of others.

Erythromycin is the one the labels treat as potent: the methylergonovine label names it among the potent CYP3A4 inhibitors and the simvastatin label groups the macrolides with the contraindicated ones. FDA's own clinical-pharmacology classification puts it with diltiazem and verapamil as MODERATE, so read the word potent here as the labels' practical judgment rather than a tier. Amlodipine is a WEAK inhibitor and is not listed here: its one labeled consequence is the simvastatin 20 mg cap, which is carried as a named pair in the miscellaneous rule.

Almost everything in this rule interferes with that trade, by removing the hormone, blocking its receptor, or blocking the sodium channel it works through, and the result is the same: potassium arrives and does not leave.

ACE inhibitors and ARBs remove aldosterone, so the kidney stops dumping K⁺. Trimethoprim blocks the distal tubule sodium channel directly, which is structurally how amiloride works. Heparin and enoxaparin suppress aldosterone synthesis in the adrenal gland, independent of their anticoagulant effect.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE and TACROLIMUS belong to the first mechanism rather than the third: the acute nephrotoxicity of a calcineurin inhibitor is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why either one plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive. They are grouped with the direct toxins because they damage the tubule as well, but the vessel is the half that acts within hours.

Gentamicin and IV vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. Route matters but does not excuse it: oral vancomycin is poorly absorbed, and yet the capsule label reports nephrotoxicity in its own controlled trials and clinically significant serum concentrations in patients with active C. difficile colitis or inflammatory bowel disease, because an inflamed colon absorbs what a healthy one does not. So check a creatinine on the oral course too, especially over 65. The IV route is the larger risk, not the only one. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses.

The kidney handles lithium exactly like sodium. Anything that reduces sodium delivery or renal blood flow makes the kidney reabsorb more lithium, and the level climbs with no change in dose. Lithium has a narrow window, so a modest rise is a real toxicity.

Read this one as a POTASSIUM pair before a creatinine pair. Spironolactone blocks aldosterone at the receptor and an ACE inhibitor or ARB removes the aldosterone signal upstream, so both halves stop the kidney dumping K⁺, and the Aldactone label names ACE inhibitors and ARBs in its hyperkalemia warning. The combination is still guideline-directed in heart failure, which is exactly why it has to be monitored rather than questioned: check K⁺ and creatinine when either drug starts or changes, and remember that the renal injury and the hyperkalemia feed each other.

Same problem as insulin and worse in one way: a sulfonylurea keeps forcing insulin out for many hours, so the hypoglycemia it causes is prolonged and recurrent, and a nonselective blocker has removed the tremor and tachycardia that would warn you AND blunted the glycogenolysis that would pull the patient back out of it. Treat diaphoresis as hypoglycemia until a glucose says otherwise.

The worst version of this pair. Nonselective blockade removes the tremor and tachycardia that tell a patient on insulin their sugar is dropping, AND blunts the beta-2 glycogenolysis that would pull it back up, so the low is both hidden and harder to escape. Sweating still comes through, because it is cholinergic, so diaphoresis is the sign to trust.

Two routes. All of them kill the gut bacteria that make vitamin K, which is the vitamin warfarin already works against, so the warfarin effect deepens. Metronidazole, Bactrim, erythromycin and isoniazid do something extra: they also block the enzyme that clears warfarin, so the drug itself builds up. Two hits instead of one is why those push the INR hardest.

RIFAMPIN is the exception that reverses the whole rule. It INDUCES the enzyme instead of blocking it, so the INR FALLS and the patient clots while looking anticoagulated on paper. See the induction rule.

The stomach lining defends itself three ways: a mucus and bicarbonate layer, blood flow to repair what gets through, and platelets to stop a bleed once one starts. Each drug here removes a different one of those, so two of them together take away both the defence and the repair.

NSAIDs remove the prostaglandins that build the mucus layer and keep the blood flowing. Steroids impair mucosal healing and mask the pain that would have warned you. SSRIs deplete platelet serotonin, so when a vessel does open there is less to plug it with: the ulcer risk they add is small, and the BLEEDING risk is the real one.

Worse than simply additive when the nephrotoxin is CYCLOSPORINE or tacrolimus, because a calcineurin inhibitor constricts the AFFERENT arteriole and an NSAID narrows the same vessel, so the two are hitting one target rather than two. The cyclosporine label says it directly: concomitant NSAIDs, particularly in the setting of dehydration, may potentiate renal dysfunction. With gentamicin or vancomycin it is additive tubular injury instead. Either way, creatinine daily and keep the patient wet.

Two routes. All of them kill the gut bacteria that make vitamin K, which is the vitamin warfarin already works against, so the warfarin effect deepens. Metronidazole, Bactrim, erythromycin and isoniazid do something extra: they also block the enzyme that clears warfarin, so the drug itself builds up. Two hits instead of one is why those push the INR hardest.

RIFAMPIN is the exception that reverses the whole rule. It INDUCES the enzyme instead of blocking it, so the INR FALLS and the patient clots while looking anticoagulated on paper. See the induction rule.

After each beat the ventricle has to repolarize, meaning reset its electrical charge, before it can beat again. Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what does that. These drugs block hERG, so repolarization drags out. That dragged-out reset is what a long QT measures, and a beat firing during that stretched window can tip the rhythm into torsades de pointes.

They do not all carry the same weight. Ondansetron, methadone, prochlorperazine, chlorpromazine, haloperidol, amitriptyline, the fluoroquinolones and the macrolides, Bactrim, and the antiarrhythmics amiodarone and procainamide are the established ones. Loperamide belongs here only at HIGHER THAN RECOMMENDED doses, which is what its boxed warning is about. For the antiarrhythmics the QT effect IS the mechanism, not a side effect, which is why a class IA or class III drug can treat an arrhythmia and cause torsades with the same action. Escitalopram, quetiapine and olanzapine prolong QT only modestly (escitalopram by about 7 msec at 20 mg), and for metronidazole the evidence is case reports while fluoxetine's effect is marginal, so treat all of those as a reason to check rather than a reason to expect it.

The SSRI with a genuinely QT-driven dose restriction is CITALOPRAM, not escitalopram.
Overlapping membership; the fluoroquinolone is already counted in the contributes group.

Low K+ and low Mg2+ lengthen the QT on their own, so they stack with a QT drug. Scoped to loop diuretics, steroids and stimulant laxatives, which drop TOTAL BODY potassium. Insulin, bicarbonate and a beta-2 agonist shift potassium into cells rather than removing it, and at routine dosing that shift is not a torsades risk on its own.

Each of these blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. One drug gives you a dry mouth. Two or three give you the full picture: blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, blocked sweating so heat cannot be shed, and in older adults an acute confusion that gets charted as dementia or a UTI rather than as the drugs.

The clinical point is that total load matters, not any single drug. This is what the Beers criteria are built around, and it is the most common reversible cause of delirium in a hospitalized older adult.

The three that most often go uncounted are DIPHENHYDRAMINE (in sleep aids and cold remedies the patient does not call medication), BENZTROPINE (given to treat the side effects of an antipsychotic that is itself anticholinergic), and PROMETHAZINE. Add any two and an older adult is at real risk.

The SSRI with a genuinely QT-driven dose restriction is CITALOPRAM, not escitalopram.

After each beat the ventricle has to repolarize, meaning reset its electrical charge, before it can beat again. Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what does that. These drugs block hERG, so repolarization drags out. That dragged-out reset is what a long QT measures, and a beat firing during that stretched window can tip the rhythm into torsades de pointes.

Two routes. All of them kill the gut bacteria that make vitamin K, which is the vitamin warfarin already works against, so the warfarin effect deepens. Metronidazole, Bactrim, erythromycin and isoniazid do something extra: they also block the enzyme that clears warfarin, so the drug itself builds up. Two hits instead of one is why those push the INR hardest.

RIFAMPIN is the exception that reverses the whole rule. It INDUCES the enzyme instead of blocking it, so the INR FALLS and the patient clots while looking anticoagulated on paper. See the induction rule.

Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.

This is a duplicate-therapy question before it is a potassium question. Two systemic steroids on one list is usually a reconciliation error or an incomplete taper, so ask which one is meant to be running.

The stomach lining defends itself three ways: a mucus and bicarbonate layer, blood flow to repair what gets through, and platelets to stop a bleed once one starts. Each drug here removes a different one of those, so two of them together take away both the defence and the repair.

NSAIDs remove the prostaglandins that build the mucus layer and keep the blood flowing. Steroids impair mucosal healing and mask the pain that would have warned you. SSRIs deplete platelet serotonin, so when a vessel does open there is less to plug it with: the ulcer risk they add is small, and the BLEEDING risk is the real one.

Digoxin works by blocking the Na+/K+ pump. Potassium competes for that same binding site, so when potassium falls, MORE digoxin binds and a level that reads therapeutic behaves like an overdose. Low magnesium does the same thing, and high calcium adds to the contractile effect digoxin is already producing.

Two different mechanisms wear this one label, and which drug you are looking at changes what you expect. A STEROID drives gluconeogenesis and blocks peripheral glucose uptake, so the insulin requirement rises steeply and predictably, highest after the morning dose and in the afternoon. A CALCINEURIN INHIBITOR, tacrolimus or cyclosporine, is doing something else: it damages the pancreatic beta cell and cuts insulin secretion, so the rise is slower, it tracks the drug level, and it does not come back down when a dose is held. Either way the trap is the TAPER rather than the start: the insulin dose that was right on 40 mg of prednisone causes hypoglycemia on 10 mg, and nobody reduces it because nothing new was ordered.

A STEROID drives gluconeogenesis and blocks peripheral glucose uptake, so the insulin requirement rises steeply and predictably, highest after the morning dose and in the afternoon. Either way the trap is the TAPER rather than the start: the insulin dose that was right on 40 mg of prednisone causes hypoglycemia on 10 mg, and nobody reduces it because nothing new was ordered.

Aldosterone is what tells the distal nephron to trade potassium away for sodium. Almost everything in this rule interferes with that trade, by removing the hormone, blocking its receptor, or blocking the sodium channel it works through, and the result is the same: potassium arrives and does not leave.

ACE inhibitors and ARBs remove aldosterone, so the kidney stops dumping K⁺. Trimethoprim blocks the distal tubule sodium channel directly, which is structurally how amiloride works. Heparin and enoxaparin suppress aldosterone synthesis in the adrenal gland, independent of their anticoagulant effect.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE and TACROLIMUS belong to the first mechanism rather than the third: the acute nephrotoxicity of a calcineurin inhibitor is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why either one plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive. They are grouped with the direct toxins because they damage the tubule as well, but the vessel is the half that acts within hours.

Gentamicin and IV vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. Route matters but does not excuse it: oral vancomycin is poorly absorbed, and yet the capsule label reports nephrotoxicity in its own controlled trials and clinically significant serum concentrations in patients with active C. difficile colitis or inflammatory bowel disease, because an inflamed colon absorbs what a healthy one does not. So check a creatinine on the oral course too, especially over 65. The IV route is the larger risk, not the only one. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses.

Every drug here can injure skeletal muscle, by routes that are mostly still argued about, and stacking two raises the chance. The sequence is what to hold on to: aching, then tenderness and weakness, then muscle breaking down fast enough to block the kidneys. The first step sounds exactly like having overdone it at the gym, which is why patients do not report it.

Statins, fibrates and niacin each injure muscle on their own, and together the risk climbs. Muscle pain and weakness are the warning. Rhabdomyolysis is the endpoint: muscle breaking down fast enough to damage the kidneys.

Why this is moderate and not high: the fibrate behind the serious cases is GEMFIBROZIL, which slows how fast the body clears a statin, so the statin builds up. Fenofibrate does not do that, which is exactly why it is the fibrate you pair with a statin. Gemfibrozil is not in this set.

How statins injure muscle at all is still unsettled. The leading explanation is that the pathway they block also supplies coenzyme Q10 to muscle.

Cyclosporine inhibits CYP3A4, so the opioid or benzodiazepine level rises; it is also a substrate, so the traffic runs both ways. Monitor sedation and respiratory rate, and check a cyclosporine level.

Worse than simply additive when the nephrotoxin is CYCLOSPORINE or tacrolimus, because a calcineurin inhibitor constricts the AFFERENT arteriole and an NSAID narrows the same vessel, so the two are hitting one target rather than two. With gentamicin or vancomycin it is additive tubular injury instead. Either way, creatinine daily and keep the patient wet.
Weak. Flagged through the fluoroquinolone link rather than on its own.

Aldosterone is what tells the distal nephron to trade potassium away for sodium. Almost everything in this rule interferes with that trade, by removing the hormone, blocking its receptor, or blocking the sodium channel it works through, and the result is the same: potassium arrives and does not leave.

ACE inhibitors and ARBs remove aldosterone, so the kidney stops dumping K⁺. Trimethoprim blocks the distal tubule sodium channel directly, which is structurally how amiloride works. Heparin and enoxaparin suppress aldosterone synthesis in the adrenal gland, independent of their anticoagulant effect.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE and TACROLIMUS belong to the first mechanism rather than the third: the acute nephrotoxicity of a calcineurin inhibitor is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why either one plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive. They are grouped with the direct toxins because they damage the tubule as well, but the vessel is the half that acts within hours.

Gentamicin and IV vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. Route matters but does not excuse it: oral vancomycin is poorly absorbed, and yet the capsule label reports nephrotoxicity in its own controlled trials and clinically significant serum concentrations in patients with active C. difficile colitis or inflammatory bowel disease, because an inflamed colon absorbs what a healthy one does not. So check a creatinine on the oral course too, especially over 65. The IV route is the larger risk, not the only one. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses.

Cyclosporine inhibits CYP3A4, so the opioid or benzodiazepine level rises; it is also a substrate, so the traffic runs both ways. Monitor sedation and respiratory rate, and check a cyclosporine level.

These inhibitors block the enzyme that clears the substrates, so the substrate accumulates at an unchanged dose. CYCLOSPORINE is in both roles: it inhibits CYP3A4 and OATP1B1, and it is itself a 3A4 substrate, so its level swings with anything that touches the enzyme and it raises the levels of others.

Erythromycin is the one the labels treat as potent: the methylergonovine label names it among the potent CYP3A4 inhibitors and the simvastatin label groups the macrolides with the contraindicated ones. FDA's own clinical-pharmacology classification puts it with diltiazem and verapamil as MODERATE, so read the word potent here as the labels' practical judgment rather than a tier. Amlodipine is a WEAK inhibitor and is not listed here: its one labeled consequence is the simvastatin 20 mg cap, which is carried as a named pair in the miscellaneous rule.

Direction depends on the dose, and the file states both because both are reported. HIGH-dose methylprednisolone and cyclosporine inhibit each other's metabolism, so the cyclosporine level RISES; at maintenance doses a steroid acts as a CYP3A4 INDUCER instead, which is why tapering prednisone off a tacrolimus patient makes that level rise (see the glucose rule). The pair is standard transplant therapy either way. What follows is not a prediction but a schedule: draw a trough after every steroid change, in either direction.

Every drug here can injure skeletal muscle, by routes that are mostly still argued about, and stacking two raises the chance. The sequence is what to hold on to: aching, then tenderness and weakness, then muscle breaking down fast enough to block the kidneys. The first step sounds exactly like having overdone it at the gym, which is why patients do not report it.

Statins, fibrates and niacin each injure muscle on their own, and together the risk climbs. Muscle pain and weakness are the warning. Rhabdomyolysis is the endpoint: muscle breaking down fast enough to damage the kidneys.

Why this is moderate and not high: the fibrate behind the serious cases is GEMFIBROZIL, which slows how fast the body clears a statin, so the statin builds up. Fenofibrate does not do that, which is exactly why it is the fibrate you pair with a statin. Gemfibrozil is not in this set.

How statins injure muscle at all is still unsettled. The leading explanation is that the pathway they block also supplies coenzyme Q10 to muscle.

Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.

Two anticoagulants may be a deliberate BRIDGE (heparin or enoxaparin overlapping warfarin until the INR is therapeutic; the 5-day parenteral lead-in dabigatran requires) or a duplication. Judge by the plan, not the count.

The stomach lining defends itself three ways: a mucus and bicarbonate layer, blood flow to repair what gets through, and platelets to stop a bleed once one starts. Each drug here removes a different one of those, so two of them together take away both the defence and the repair.

NSAIDs remove the prostaglandins that build the mucus layer and keep the blood flowing. Steroids impair mucosal healing and mask the pain that would have warned you. SSRIs deplete platelet serotonin, so when a vessel does open there is less to plug it with: the ulcer risk they add is small, and the BLEEDING risk is the real one.

Low K+ and low Mg2+ lengthen the QT on their own, so they stack with a QT drug. Scoped to loop diuretics, steroids and stimulant laxatives, which drop TOTAL BODY potassium. Insulin, bicarbonate and a beta-2 agonist shift potassium into cells rather than removing it, and at routine dosing that shift is not a torsades risk on its own.

Two different mechanisms wear this one label, and which drug you are looking at changes what you expect. A STEROID drives gluconeogenesis and blocks peripheral glucose uptake, so the insulin requirement rises steeply and predictably, highest after the morning dose and in the afternoon. A CALCINEURIN INHIBITOR, tacrolimus or cyclosporine, is doing something else: it damages the pancreatic beta cell and cuts insulin secretion, so the rise is slower, it tracks the drug level, and it does not come back down when a dose is held. Either way the trap is the TAPER rather than the start: the insulin dose that was right on 40 mg of prednisone causes hypoglycemia on 10 mg, and nobody reduces it because nothing new was ordered.
Different mechanisms and both weak. Insulin shifts potassium into cells and dexamethasone barely touches it, so a low K⁺ here is usually something else.

Erythromycin roughly DOUBLES digoxin exposure, by two routes at once: it inhibits the P-glycoprotein that pumps digoxin out, and it kills the colonic bacteria that inactivate a share of each oral dose. Check a digoxin level and watch for nausea, visual halos and bradycardia.

Digoxin works by blocking the Na+/K+ pump. Potassium competes for that same binding site, so when potassium falls, MORE digoxin binds and a level that reads therapeutic behaves like an overdose. Low magnesium does the same thing, and high calcium adds to the contractile effect digoxin is already producing.

Digoxin works by blocking the Na+/K+ pump. Potassium competes for that same binding site, so when potassium falls, MORE digoxin binds and a level that reads therapeutic behaves like an overdose. The potassium does not have to leave the body to make digoxin toxic. What the Na+/K+ pump competes with is the potassium in the SERUM, so insulin, bicarbonate or a beta-2 nebulizer driving it into cells frees up binding sites within the hour, and a level that reads therapeutic starts behaving like an overdose. Two things follow. Treating hyperkalemia in a digitalized patient can tip them into toxicity, so the ECG matters as much as the next potassium. And the number comes back up on its own as the drug wears off, so a single low K⁺ drawn mid-nebulizer is not the whole picture.

Labeled, and it is a LEVEL interaction rather than a potassium one, which is what makes it easy to miss: spironolactone raises digoxin exposure by around 44 percent by competing for the P-glycoprotein transporter that clears it, so the level climbs with no dose change. It also interferes with some older digoxin immunoassays, so a reported level can be wrong in either direction. The pair is common in heart failure; the action is to recheck the level after spironolactone starts.

Named on the nifedipine label: diltiazem raises nifedipine exposure 2.2 to 3.1 fold, so the nifedipine dose should be reduced. This is a pharmacokinetic interaction on top of the additive blood pressure effect, and it is the bigger of the two.

A dihydropyridine WITH a beta blocker is deliberate and common: the beta blocker cancels the reflex tachycardia nifedipine causes, so the pair is better than either alone. Watch BP and standing symptoms, and note this is the opposite of diltiazem or verapamil with a beta blocker, which stacks AV block.

These inhibitors block the enzyme that clears the substrates, so the substrate accumulates at an unchanged dose. CYCLOSPORINE is in both roles: it inhibits CYP3A4 and OATP1B1, and it is itself a 3A4 substrate, so its level swings with anything that touches the enzyme and it raises the levels of others.

Erythromycin is the one the labels treat as potent: the methylergonovine label names it among the potent CYP3A4 inhibitors and the simvastatin label groups the macrolides with the contraindicated ones. FDA's own clinical-pharmacology classification puts it with diltiazem and verapamil as MODERATE, so read the word potent here as the labels' practical judgment rather than a tier. Amlodipine is a WEAK inhibitor and is not listed here: its one labeled consequence is the simvastatin 20 mg cap, which is carried as a named pair in the miscellaneous rule.

A beta blocker works by sitting on the receptor. Anything else you give that needs the SAME receptor then has to compete for it, so the dose that normally works does less than expected, and how much less depends on which receptor and how selective the blocker is. That cuts two ways in this rule: a pressor that cannot raise the pressure, and a rescue inhaler that cannot open the airway.

Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine and dobutamine all work through adrenergic receptors. A beta blocker already occupying those receptors reduces the response. With epinephrine the picture is worse: beta blockade leaves alpha effects unopposed, which can produce severe hypertension with reflex bradycardia.
Beta blockade reduces the response to a pressor, and with epinephrine it leaves alpha effects unopposed, which can produce severe hypertension with reflex bradycardia.

Catecholamines are stable in acid and destroyed in base. Mixed with sodium bicarbonate, or run into a line that bicarbonate is running through, they oxidize and lose activity. The infusion keeps running, the pump keeps counting, and the patient gets nothing.

This is chemical degradation rather than a pharmacologic interaction, and it is OXIDATION rather than precipitation: the catecholamine is converted to inactive adrenochrome. That distinction matters at the bedside, because there may be no particulate to find. Checking the line for precipitate is not a valid safety check here. The only signs are a pressor requirement that climbs for no clinical reason, and sometimes a solution that has turned pink or brown. In a code, where bicarbonate and epinephrine are both being given, the answer is to flush the line between them or use a second access.

Furosemide injection has a pH of 8.0 to 9.3 and is documented incompatible with dopamine. Note this is dopamine-specific: epinephrine and norepinephrine are listed as Y-site compatible with furosemide, so do not generalize it to the whole group.
Additive catecholamine effect, and dopamine at pressor doses raises blood pressure through the same alpha receptors.

Two routes. All of them kill the gut bacteria that make vitamin K, which is the vitamin warfarin already works against, so the warfarin effect deepens. Metronidazole, Bactrim, erythromycin and isoniazid do something extra: they also block the enzyme that clears warfarin, so the drug itself builds up. Two hits instead of one is why those push the INR hardest.

RIFAMPIN is the exception that reverses the whole rule. It INDUCES the enzyme instead of blocking it, so the INR FALLS and the patient clots while looking anticoagulated on paper. See the induction rule.

Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.

Too much serotonin at the synapse. The SSRIs and SNRIs here (fluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram, venlafaxine, duloxetine) raise it directly by blocking its reuptake. Amitriptyline does the same, alongside norepinephrine. Methadone and buspirone contribute weakly.

Ondansetron and metoclopramide are a different case. They BLOCK serotonin receptors rather than raising serotonin, and the link to serotonin syndrome rests on case reports with no established mechanism. Treat them as a reason to look, not a reason to expect it.

The stomach lining defends itself three ways: a mucus and bicarbonate layer, blood flow to repair what gets through, and platelets to stop a bleed once one starts. Each drug here removes a different one of those, so two of them together take away both the defence and the repair.

NSAIDs remove the prostaglandins that build the mucus layer and keep the blood flowing. Steroids impair mucosal healing and mask the pain that would have warned you. SSRIs deplete platelet serotonin, so when a vessel does open there is less to plug it with: the ulcer risk they add is small, and the BLEEDING risk is the real one.

Aldosterone is what tells the distal nephron to trade potassium away for sodium. Almost everything in this rule interferes with that trade, by removing the hormone, blocking its receptor, or blocking the sodium channel it works through, and the result is the same: potassium arrives and does not leave.

ACE inhibitors and ARBs remove aldosterone, so the kidney stops dumping K⁺. Trimethoprim blocks the distal tubule sodium channel directly, which is structurally how amiloride works. Heparin and enoxaparin suppress aldosterone synthesis in the adrenal gland, independent of their anticoagulant effect.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE and TACROLIMUS belong to the first mechanism rather than the third: the acute nephrotoxicity of a calcineurin inhibitor is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why either one plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive. They are grouped with the direct toxins because they damage the tubule as well, but the vessel is the half that acts within hours.

Gentamicin and IV vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. Route matters but does not excuse it: oral vancomycin is poorly absorbed, and yet the capsule label reports nephrotoxicity in its own controlled trials and clinically significant serum concentrations in patients with active C. difficile colitis or inflammatory bowel disease, because an inflamed colon absorbs what a healthy one does not. So check a creatinine on the oral course too, especially over 65. The IV route is the larger risk, not the only one. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses.

Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.

Additive adrenergic effect on heart rate and blood pressure. The methylphenidate label advises caution with pressor agents.

A beta blocker works by sitting on the receptor. Anything else you give that needs the SAME receptor then has to compete for it, so the dose that normally works does less than expected, and how much less depends on which receptor and how selective the blocker is. That cuts two ways in this rule: a pressor that cannot raise the pressure, and a rescue inhaler that cannot open the airway.

Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine and dobutamine all work through adrenergic receptors. A beta blocker already occupying those receptors reduces the response. With epinephrine the picture is worse: beta blockade leaves alpha effects unopposed, which can produce severe hypertension with reflex bradycardia.
Beta blockade reduces the response to a pressor, and with epinephrine it leaves alpha effects unopposed, which can produce severe hypertension with reflex bradycardia.

Catecholamines are stable in acid and destroyed in base. Mixed with sodium bicarbonate, or run into a line that bicarbonate is running through, they oxidize and lose activity. The infusion keeps running, the pump keeps counting, and the patient gets nothing.

This is chemical degradation rather than a pharmacologic interaction, and it is OXIDATION rather than precipitation: the catecholamine is converted to inactive adrenochrome. That distinction matters at the bedside, because there may be no particulate to find. Checking the line for precipitate is not a valid safety check here. The only signs are a pressor requirement that climbs for no clinical reason, and sometimes a solution that has turned pink or brown. In a code, where bicarbonate and epinephrine are both being given, the answer is to flush the line between them or use a second access.

After each beat the ventricle has to repolarize, meaning reset its electrical charge, before it can beat again. Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what does that. These drugs block hERG, so repolarization drags out. That dragged-out reset is what a long QT measures, and a beat firing during that stretched window can tip the rhythm into torsades de pointes.

They do not all carry the same weight. Ondansetron, methadone, prochlorperazine, chlorpromazine, haloperidol, amitriptyline, the fluoroquinolones and the macrolides, Bactrim, and the antiarrhythmics amiodarone and procainamide are the established ones. Loperamide belongs here only at HIGHER THAN RECOMMENDED doses, which is what its boxed warning is about. For the antiarrhythmics the QT effect IS the mechanism, not a side effect, which is why a class IA or class III drug can treat an arrhythmia and cause torsades with the same action. Escitalopram, quetiapine and olanzapine prolong QT only modestly (escitalopram by about 7 msec at 20 mg), and for metronidazole the evidence is case reports while fluoxetine's effect is marginal, so treat all of those as a reason to check rather than a reason to expect it.

The SSRI with a genuinely QT-driven dose restriction is CITALOPRAM, not escitalopram.

Weaker on both sides, and IV vancomycin is the route that matters: the ototoxicity reports are with excessive intravenous doses, not with the oral capsules for C. difficile. Worth noting in a patient already getting high-dose IV vancomycin with aggressive diuresis, and not otherwise.

The hair cells of the cochlea and the vestibular apparatus do not regenerate. Aminoglycosides accumulate in them and kill them. Loop diuretics damage the same structures through the ion pump in the inner ear, and high-dose IV erythromycin and vancomycin add to it.

That is the asymmetry worth holding on to, and it is about the AMINOGLYCOSIDE above all: the kidney injury gentamicin causes is usually reversible, and the hearing loss it causes usually is not. So a rising creatinine is a reason to adjust, while tinnitus is a reason to stop and call.

Not every drug here carries that prognosis. Salicylate ototoxicity is dose-dependent and reverses within days of stopping, and the loop diuretic and erythromycin effects are usually reversible too. The nursing action does not change, because you cannot tell at the bedside which kind of tinnitus you are hearing, and the one you cannot take back is the one you have to assume.

These inhibitors block the enzyme that clears the substrates, so the substrate accumulates at an unchanged dose. CYCLOSPORINE is in both roles: it inhibits CYP3A4 and OATP1B1, and it is itself a 3A4 substrate, so its level swings with anything that touches the enzyme and it raises the levels of others.

Erythromycin is the one the labels treat as potent: the methylergonovine label names it among the potent CYP3A4 inhibitors and the simvastatin label groups the macrolides with the contraindicated ones. FDA's own clinical-pharmacology classification puts it with diltiazem and verapamil as MODERATE, so read the word potent here as the labels' practical judgment rather than a tier. Amlodipine is a WEAK inhibitor and is not listed here: its one labeled consequence is the simvastatin 20 mg cap, which is carried as a named pair in the miscellaneous rule.

These inhibitors block the enzyme that clears the substrates, so the substrate accumulates at an unchanged dose. CYCLOSPORINE is in both roles: it inhibits CYP3A4 and OATP1B1, and it is itself a 3A4 substrate, so its level swings with anything that touches the enzyme and it raises the levels of others.

Erythromycin is the one the labels treat as potent: the methylergonovine label names it among the potent CYP3A4 inhibitors and the simvastatin label groups the macrolides with the contraindicated ones. FDA's own clinical-pharmacology classification puts it with diltiazem and verapamil as MODERATE, so read the word potent here as the labels' practical judgment rather than a tier. Amlodipine is a WEAK inhibitor and is not listed here: its one labeled consequence is the simvastatin 20 mg cap, which is carried as a named pair in the miscellaneous rule.

Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.

The stomach lining defends itself three ways: a mucus and bicarbonate layer, blood flow to repair what gets through, and platelets to stop a bleed once one starts. Each drug here removes a different one of those, so two of them together take away both the defence and the repair.

NSAIDs remove the prostaglandins that build the mucus layer and keep the blood flowing. Steroids impair mucosal healing and mask the pain that would have warned you. SSRIs deplete platelet serotonin, so when a vessel does open there is less to plug it with: the ulcer risk they add is small, and the BLEEDING risk is the real one.

NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.

Too much serotonin at the synapse. The SSRIs and SNRIs here (fluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram, venlafaxine, duloxetine) raise it directly by blocking its reuptake. Amitriptyline does the same, alongside norepinephrine. Methadone and buspirone contribute weakly.

Ondansetron and metoclopramide are a different case. They BLOCK serotonin receptors rather than raising serotonin, and the link to serotonin syndrome rests on case reports with no established mechanism. Treat them as a reason to look, not a reason to expect it.

The stomach lining defends itself three ways: a mucus and bicarbonate layer, blood flow to repair what gets through, and platelets to stop a bleed once one starts. Each drug here removes a different one of those, so two of them together take away both the defence and the repair.

NSAIDs remove the prostaglandins that build the mucus layer and keep the blood flowing. Steroids impair mucosal healing and mask the pain that would have warned you. SSRIs deplete platelet serotonin, so when a vessel does open there is less to plug it with: the ulcer risk they add is small, and the BLEEDING risk is the real one.

After each beat the ventricle has to repolarize, meaning reset its electrical charge, before it can beat again. Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what does that. These drugs block hERG, so repolarization drags out. That dragged-out reset is what a long QT measures, and a beat firing during that stretched window can tip the rhythm into torsades de pointes.

They do not all carry the same weight. Ondansetron, methadone, prochlorperazine, chlorpromazine, haloperidol, amitriptyline, the fluoroquinolones and the macrolides, Bactrim, and the antiarrhythmics amiodarone and procainamide are the established ones. Loperamide belongs here only at HIGHER THAN RECOMMENDED doses, which is what its boxed warning is about. For the antiarrhythmics the QT effect IS the mechanism, not a side effect, which is why a class IA or class III drug can treat an arrhythmia and cause torsades with the same action. Escitalopram, quetiapine and olanzapine prolong QT only modestly (escitalopram by about 7 msec at 20 mg), and for metronidazole the evidence is case reports while fluoxetine's effect is marginal, so treat all of those as a reason to check rather than a reason to expect it.

The SSRI with a genuinely QT-driven dose restriction is CITALOPRAM, not escitalopram.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE and TACROLIMUS belong to the first mechanism rather than the third: the acute nephrotoxicity of a calcineurin inhibitor is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why either one plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive. They are grouped with the direct toxins because they damage the tubule as well, but the vessel is the half that acts within hours.

Gentamicin and IV vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. Route matters but does not excuse it: oral vancomycin is poorly absorbed, and yet the capsule label reports nephrotoxicity in its own controlled trials and clinically significant serum concentrations in patients with active C. difficile colitis or inflammatory bowel disease, because an inflamed colon absorbs what a healthy one does not. So check a creatinine on the oral course too, especially over 65. The IV route is the larger risk, not the only one. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses.

The hair cells of the cochlea and the vestibular apparatus do not regenerate. Aminoglycosides accumulate in them and kill them. Loop diuretics damage the same structures through the ion pump in the inner ear, and high-dose IV erythromycin and vancomycin add to it.

That is the asymmetry worth holding on to, and it is about the AMINOGLYCOSIDE above all: the kidney injury gentamicin causes is usually reversible, and the hearing loss it causes usually is not. So a rising creatinine is a reason to adjust, while tinnitus is a reason to stop and call.

Not every drug here carries that prognosis. Salicylate ototoxicity is dose-dependent and reverses within days of stopping, and the loop diuretic and erythromycin effects are usually reversible too. The nursing action does not change, because you cannot tell at the bedside which kind of tinnitus you are hearing, and the one you cannot take back is the one you have to assume.

The hair cells of the cochlea and the vestibular apparatus do not regenerate. Aminoglycosides accumulate in them and kill them. Loop diuretics damage the same structures through the ion pump in the inner ear, and high-dose IV erythromycin and vancomycin add to it.

That is the asymmetry worth holding on to, and it is about the AMINOGLYCOSIDE above all: the kidney injury gentamicin causes is usually reversible, and the hearing loss it causes usually is not. So a rising creatinine is a reason to adjust, while tinnitus is a reason to stop and call.

Not every drug here carries that prognosis. Salicylate ototoxicity is dose-dependent and reverses within days of stopping, and the loop diuretic and erythromycin effects are usually reversible too. The nursing action does not change, because you cannot tell at the bedside which kind of tinnitus you are hearing, and the one you cannot take back is the one you have to assume.

After each beat the ventricle has to repolarize, meaning reset its electrical charge, before it can beat again. Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what does that. Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.

Aldosterone is what tells the distal nephron to trade potassium away for sodium. Almost everything in this rule interferes with that trade, by removing the hormone, blocking its receptor, or blocking the sodium channel it works through, and the result is the same: potassium arrives and does not leave.

ACE inhibitors and ARBs remove aldosterone, so the kidney stops dumping K⁺. Trimethoprim blocks the distal tubule sodium channel directly, which is structurally how amiloride works. Heparin and enoxaparin suppress aldosterone synthesis in the adrenal gland, independent of their anticoagulant effect.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE and TACROLIMUS belong to the first mechanism rather than the third: the acute nephrotoxicity of a calcineurin inhibitor is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why either one plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive. They are grouped with the direct toxins because they damage the tubule as well, but the vessel is the half that acts within hours.

Gentamicin and IV vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. Route matters but does not excuse it: oral vancomycin is poorly absorbed, and yet the capsule label reports nephrotoxicity in its own controlled trials and clinically significant serum concentrations in patients with active C. difficile colitis or inflammatory bowel disease, because an inflamed colon absorbs what a healthy one does not. So check a creatinine on the oral course too, especially over 65. The IV route is the larger risk, not the only one. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses.

Antihypertensives and diuretics rely partly on prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation and renal sodium handling. NSAIDs block prostaglandin synthesis, so the BP drug works less well and sodium is retained.

That mechanism is what sets the scope. The nitrates are not here: they donate nitric oxide directly, so there is no prostaglandin step to block, and they are titrated to an effect you can see rather than trusted to hold a pressure over weeks. The dihydropyridines, nifedipine and amlodipine, are the least affected of the ones that are listed, because they do not depend on prostaglandins either; what reaches them is the sodium and water the NSAID makes the kidney keep.

Potassium can leave the blood two ways, and the lab draw looks the same either way. It can leave the BODY, through the kidney or the gut, which is a true deficit that has to be replaced. Or it can move INTO the cells, which is a shift that reverses on its own when the drug wears off. Replacing a shift overshoots; ignoring a deficit does not correct.

Loop diuretics dump K⁺ at the loop of Henle. Prednisone, methylprednisolone and cortisone hold Na⁺ and trade away K⁺ through mineralocorticoid activity. Dexamethasone has almost none of that activity, so its hypokalemia is weaker and arrives by other routes at high dose, which is why it sits in a group of its own here. Insulin, sodium bicarbonate and a beta-2 agonist don't remove potassium at all, they drive it into cells, which looks identical on a lab draw and corrects itself when the drug wears off.

A beta-2 agonist drives potassium and glucose in the same direction insulin is fighting, and a thiazide raises glucose over weeks. Expect the insulin requirement to move, and check more often rather than treating it as an error.

SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.
